explicaciones.texto: "Have" is an irregular verb. The third person singular form is "has," not "haves." Use "has" for the third person singular (he, she, or it).
These pronouns take "have": I, You, We, They. These pronouns take "has": He, She, It. Structure: SUBJECT + "HAVE"/"HAS" + OBJECT.

Although "have" is irregular, its negative is formed in the usual way. The negative form can also be contracted as with other verbs. Use "does not" instead of "do not" for she, he, and it. "Do not" can be shortened to "don't." "Does not" can be shortened to "doesn't." Always use "have" instead of "has" in the negative.

explicaciones.texto: Use "can" to talk about the things you are able to do, such as ride a bicycle or play the guitar. Use "cannot" or "can't" for things you are not able to do. "Can't" is the short form of "cannot". Tip: the long negative form "cannot" is always spelled as one word, not two words.

explicaciones.texto: If you do something "quite" well, you're OK but not excellent at it. If you do it "very" or "really" well, you're excellent. "Quite" modifies the main adverb, "well," and goes before it.

explicaciones.titulo: KEY LANGUAGE Modifying adverbs with "good at"
explicaciones.texto: You can also use modifying adverbs with the phrases "good at" and "bad at." "Quite" modifies "good at." Remember that "good at" and "bad at" are followed by a gerund. "Very / really" goes before "good at."

explicaciones.titulo: KEY LANGUAGE "I WOULD LIKE / I WANT"
explicaciones.texto: You can use "I want" and "I would like" to talk about things you want to do. You can also use their negative form to say what you would not like to do. "I would like" is similar to "I want," but "I want" is stronger.
